brief.head: Friends by choice
brief.text: The internet let Amit Varma’s “cusp generation” move from communities of circumstance to communities of choice, he said. Almost all his close friends now come from the latter. {126-C01}

brief.head: Body and mind apart
brief.text: In women, physical and psychological arousal are separate processes, Amit Varma said. So a body’s response during rape is not consent, nor secret enjoyment. {126-C12}

brief.head: Clever, for her sake
brief.text: Where females are choosy, males must compete. “In humans, men are smart because women are selective,” Amit Varma said; Steven Pinker suggests art may be male ornamentation. {126-C17}

brief.head: Green-eyed, two ways
brief.text: Male jealousy is sexual, female jealousy emotional, Amit Varma said. With conditioning and patriarchy, he thinks this partly explains why wives forgive infidelity more often than husbands. {126-C16}

brief.head: Lovable beats great
brief.text: Women want to be lovable, men aspire for greatness, Amit Varma said. He called the male chase toxic and an obstacle to happiness: men should aspire to be lovable too. {126-C18}

thought.text: Men love women, women love children, children love kittens.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, recalling a “pretty line” at the close; Amit Varma noted there was no reciprocity

lead.kicker: Amit Varma reads the evolutionary science of desire
lead.head: He wants pictures, she wants plots
body: Amit Varma had already given this talk once, at a Goa meetup of Life Lessons, the online course he runs with Ajay Shah. He warned the room that it was “not a practical class, but theory, theory.” {126-J01}
In Episode 126 of *Everything is Everything*, he gave it again for Shah: the what and the why of human sexuality, drawn largely from one book, *A Billion Wicked Thoughts* by Ogi Ogas and Say Gaddam.

Where Alfred Kinsey asked people what they did, the book looks at what they do online: what men and women search for, and what romance novels sell. “Scientists have an easier time gazing at intergalactic quasars than peeking into someone’s bedroom,” its authors write.
## Two different bets
The root, Varma said, lies in hunter-gatherer times. Spreading his genes cost a man nothing. A woman paid with nine months of pregnancy and years of child-rearing, and got only a few shots. {126-C06}
So men are wired to seek quantity and women to be selective, choosing both good genes and a reliable provider. From this, Varma said, flows nearly every difference between the sexes.
He insisted it was “a description, not a prescription”.
The book’s headline finding follows, as Varma put it: “men are into visual cues and images, women are into stories and narratives.”
## Clips and paperbacks
The evidence is in behaviour. When the book was written, Varma said, about 2 per cent of credit-card payments for porn came from women. About 90 per cent of romance novels are read by women.
Ogas and Gaddam put the contrast starkly. A 60-second clip can be enough for a man, but the most popular aid to women’s arousal is a 250-page book “that requires hours to digest”. {126-C10}
In women’s minds, the authors say, runs “Miss Marple’s detective agency”: social, cultural, emotional and physical detectives vetting every suitor. Men have only the physical one.

Hence what they call the power of or and the power of and. One cue can be enough for a man. For a woman, looks, conversation, attention and status must all line up. “Is he a chauffeur or is he a CEO?” Varma asked. {126-C13}
Romance novels, Varma said, reveal women’s preferences as porn reveals men’s. Their heroes are dominant, rich and, in the end, tamed.
## Agency, not destiny
Why study any of this? Understanding human nature, Varma said, “increases both our agency and our compassion”. Both hosts, he noted, are hardwired to want children, and both chose not to have any.
He asked listeners not to leap from what is natural to what is right, and Shah reminded them that an average is not an identity.
Varma closed with Madame de Staël, whose line he thinks lies at the heart of human sexuality: “The desire of the man is for the woman. The desire of the woman is for the desire of the man.” {126-C20}

Shah had the last serious word. Traditional society wrapped sexuality in inhibition, he said, and modern social media culture enforces “very old fashioned norms”, in many peculiar ways more toxically.
He urged readers to read the book all the same. “A lot of it is uncomfortable,” he said.

second.label: Intelligence
second.head: Licence to remember
second.deck: Ajay Shah says women who helped hunt bin Laden hold a lesson for India
body: Intelligence operatives, in our mental model, are men out of a John le Carré book or a James Bond movie, Ajay Shah said. Yet the traits Amit Varma had just described in women would work extremely well in the field.

Varma had argued that women tend to have better memories and a sharper eye for detail. In the CIA’s hunt for Osama bin Laden, Shah said, critical persons were women, able to hold vast databases in their heads and spot what fell out of pattern. {126-S04}
India, he said, should rebuild its intelligence forces with many, many women hires. It sounded glib, Varma said, but both of them meant it seriously. {#glib}

quote.text: They had that ability to hold vast databases in their head and see one thing falling out of pattern.

second.caption: the women who hunted bin Laden

third.head: Fowl play in the barnyard
body: Sometimes, Amit Varma said, visual cues matter so much that the woman doesn’t matter at all. He read from *A Billion Wicked Thoughts* on biologists testing which cues set off mating behaviour in male fowl. {126-C09}

“About half of all roosters attempted copulation with an artificial chicken head mounted on a feather covered board.” Turkeys were less discriminating still: male gobblers will try to mate with a rubber ball of the size and height of a female head.
Varma saw the same logic in hentai, a kind of anime in which every cue is exaggerated. {#hentai}

Ajay Shah offered an analogy: porn thrived when screens were 640 by 480 pixels, and was “always the pioneering app that drove computer usage”. Varma recalled dial-up days, waiting for a picture of Samantha Fox to load. {126-J07}
third.caption: the roosters and the feathered board

p2.title: The wiring of desire
p2.deck: Amit Varma walks Ajay Shah through the evolutionary science of sex, from Kinsey to the romance aisle

sections.label: The what and why
sections.head: From questionnaires to clicks
sections.caption: the what and the why of sexuality
body: To understand sexuality, Amit Varma said, we need two things: what we are, and why we are that way. Neither is well understood. “We know very little about our own sexual desires, we are in denial of a lot of them.”

The what began with Alfred Kinsey, who, Varma said, put 521 questions to many thousands of respondents. {#kinsey521} His books on men and women overturned myths about homosexuality and female pleasure.
But his respondents came from elite Westernised society, and they were stating their preferences. {#elite}
## The why

The why came from evolution. After Richard Dawkins’s *The Selfish Gene* in 1975, Varma said, the next big milestone was Donald Symons’s *The Evolution of Human Sexuality* in 1979, which used natural selection to explain why men and women are wired differently. {126-R05}

Varma also read Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate* and books that built on Symons: Geoffrey Miller’s *The Mating Mind*, David Buss’s *The Evolution of Desire*, Robert Wright’s *The Moral Animal*. None of them, he said, treats nature and nurture as a binary. {126-C21}
*A Billion Wicked Thoughts* joins the strands. It studies anonymised online behaviour, from porn searches to romance readership, and explains it with natural selection, psychology and sociology.
~ Varma called this a book episode, in the line of earlier ones on Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson* and James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*.

quote.text: he was right so trivially that today it boggles the mind that he was treated the way he was.

sections.label: Four reasons
sections.head: Know thyself, then others
sections.caption: why sexuality is worth knowing
body: People often talk about sex almost guiltily, Amit Varma said, but it is core to understanding ourselves. He gave four reasons to study it.

The first is the inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi: know thyself. {126-J15} Otherwise, he said, we gaslight ourselves about our urges. Before we can be kind to others, we must be kind to ourselves; before that, we must know ourselves.

The second is to know others, instead of judging them by our own instincts. He quoted Donald Symons: “To encounter erotica designed to appeal to the other sex is to gaze into the psychological abyss that separates the sexes.” {126-J16}
## Agency and mismatch
Third, knowing our wiring lets us override it. Everyone is hardwired to have kids, Varma said; he and Ajay Shah decided not to have any. {126-C02}

Fourth, our instincts were built for hunter-gatherer times and are mismatched with the modern world. Ogas and Gaddam write that “porn, dating apps and birth control hijack ancient circuits meant for scarcity and reproduction.” {#hijack}
~ Varma admitted to violent instincts of his own, which he has learned not to act on. He is, he said, “fully Bengali, but in traffic I become a Punjabi.”

quote.text: I believe understanding human nature increases both our agency and our compassion.

sections.label: Four caveats
sections.head: Ought, is and the rasgulla
sections.caption: reading nature without misreading it
body: Amit Varma said he was terrified that clips from the episode would circulate without context, so he began with four caveats. {#clips}

First, the is-ought problem, which he attributed to David Hume. If men are wired to be promiscuous, it does not follow that they should be. We are hardwired for violence too. “You do not get to an ought from an is.” {126-C03}

Second, the naturalistic fallacy, a term he credited to G. E. Moore, around 1903: treating natural as good. Bigots once called homosexuality unnatural and therefore bad. It is perfectly natural in our species and many others, Varma said, and the argument would be a fallacy even if it were not.
## Proximate and ultimate

Third, do not confuse proximate causes with ultimate ones. We like sweets because, when calories were unpredictable, those who stocked up survived. {126-C04} But Ajay Shah, Varma said, “likes a rasgulla today because he just does.”
Fourth, every generalisation has exceptions. Shah made the point with shoe sizes: on average older children have bigger feet, yet five-year-olds vary enormously among themselves. {#shoesize}
~ Varma had joked on the course’s WhatsApp group that members read a paper a day on average: 139 read none and Shah reads 140 a night. Shah said he averages three a week. {126-J02}

quote.text: So on average, something can be true, but that’s not our essential identity.

sections.label: The root of it
sections.head: Sow widely, choose wisely
sections.caption: promiscuous men and selective women
body: Before turning to the book, Amit Varma set out what the field already agrees on. Its first two points go together: men are wired to be promiscuous, women to be selective. {126-C06}

In hunter-gatherer times, he said, a man’s incentive was to spread his genes as widely as possible, “and there is no cost to spreading his genes. Not for him.” A woman faced pregnancy and years of raising a baby, with no pill and no rhythm method.
So women select in two ways, Varma said: for men whose genes are likely to spread, and for a man who will look after mother and child. These are often two different men.
## Youth, status, romance
From the asymmetry, he argued, comes the next pair. Men are drawn to youth and beauty, signs of present and future fertility. Women are drawn to status and power, to the chief of the tribe.

Romance and jealousy are adaptations too, keeping a family together around the child. Robert Wright’s *The Moral Animal*, Varma said, shows how such impulses can settle into monogamy or polygamy, depending on a society’s direction. {#wright}
~ None of this is a value judgement, he stressed. “It’s not justification. It’s just explanation.”

quote.text: Men are wired to be promiscuous, women are wired to be selective.

sections.label: Men and images
sections.head: What the search bar knows
sections.caption: men’s searches and fertility cues
body: Men prefer visual cues, Amit Varma said, and what they look for are signs of youth and fertility. Porn searches reveal what men like, not what they say they like.

Ornaments such as the peacock’s tail attract mates even when they attract predators. In humans, beauty signals health: ideal female faces differ across cultures, but all are symmetrical. “We find symmetry beautiful because it is a sign of good health.” {126-C07}
Searches for “fat” or “overweight” outnumber those for “skinny” three to one. {#fat} The skinny ideal, Ogas and Gaddam suggest, comes from women’s magazines such as *Vogue* and *Cosmopolitan*.
Men prefer a waist-to-hip ratio of 0.7 without ever searching for hips. In an English bar, a woman was hit on far more often as padding took her from an A cup to a C cup. {#acup}
## The small-feet puzzle

Varma had long wondered why feet are erotic in almost every culture. The answer: healthy oestrogen levels produce gynoid fat in breasts and buttocks, and small feet, so the three go together. {#gynoid}
Nobody thinks about oestrogen, he said: “we are just drawn to these areas of the human body without ever actually knowing why.” {126-C08}
~ Varma, who says he is not drawn to small feet himself, counts as one of the exceptions.

quote.text: our instincts are hardwired in such a way that we are drawn to these signs of fertility

sections.label: Women and stories
sections.head: Taming the wild coconut
sections.caption: romance as the porn for women
body: “Romance is to women what porn is to men,” Amit Varma said. Romance is the largest genre in fiction by far, and about 90 per cent of romance novels are read by women. {#ninety}

He quizzed Ajay Shah on *The Flame and the Flower*, which he called the first romance novel published straight to paperback, after which the genre took off. Shah, in the post-lunch blues, did not guess.

The novels reveal women’s preferences as porn reveals men’s, Varma said. Heroes are dominant, and the central fantasy is taming the wild coconut. “A coconut is something that is hard on the outside and soft on the inside.” {#coconut}
Status matters too. Ogas and Gaddam counted 415 millionaires, 286 billionaires and 263 sheikhs in romance titles on Amazon. {126-C14}
## Two delusions
Each sex, Varma said, has its great self-delusion. For women, it is finding the exciting bad boy and the steady provider in one man. For men, it is that they can reliably satisfy a woman. {126-C15}
~ Seldom, he said, can anyone combine “the sexual allure of the younger Ajay Shah and the responsible vibe of the older Ajay Shah”. {126-J11}

quote.text: the great self delusion for women is that they can get both the men in one body.

side.boxText: *A Billion Wicked Thoughts*, by Ogi Ogas and Say Gaddam, studies what people search for and read online, not what they tell researchers. Amit Varma read a physical copy, underlined nearly every page, and said it made what he knew intuitively “high definition”. {126-R01}

contQuote.text: Sometimes nurture amplifies nature, sometimes it mitigates nature, which is to my mind the project of civilisation, to mitigate the worst instincts of our hard wiring and choose who we want to be and live accordingly.

stories.start: I want to take you back to the middle of the twentieth century
stories.end: today it boggles the mind that he was treated the way he was
stories.caption: Alfred Kinsey’s fate
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the man who asked America about sex
stories.head: Right too soon, and paid for it
body: In the middle of the twentieth century, a researcher called Alfred Kinsey set out to discover what human sexuality is: what urges people have and how they behave. He put, Amit Varma said, 521 questions to many thousands of respondents.

The results busted myths. People believed homosexuality was fringe, deviant behaviour practised by very few. His survey found that as many as a third of men admitted to a homosexual experience. {#third}

The notion that women did not really feel sexual pleasure fell too. A significant chunk of women, Varma said, masturbated, thought about sex and slept with men other than their husbands. “That’s awesome. It’s a celebration of sexuality.”

The findings on women were not palatable to society, even in America. The volume on men appeared in 1948 and the one on women in 1953, at which point the Rockefeller Foundation dropped his funding. {#rockefeller} Varma thought he could no longer teach at his university either, though he did not remember the details.
Kinsey died at 62, of pneumonia. {#sixtytwo} “But I have no doubt that there was a lot of pain for him in his last years because no one took his work seriously,” Varma said.

Kinsey had his limits, Varma allowed: his respondents were elite and Westernised, and stated their preferences rather than revealing them. Yet he was right, Varma said, so obviously that his treatment now boggles the mind. {126-S02}

~ Varma likened him to Ignaz Semmelweis, who first exposed the importance of hand-washing before surgery. No one took him seriously, people kept dying, and Semmelweis died in a lunatic asylum. {#semmelweis}
stories.why: Those who report uncomfortable truths are often punished in their lifetimes and vindicated so completely afterwards that their treatment looks absurd. What one generation finds unspeakable, a later one may find obvious.

stories.start: So I have to tell you an interesting tidbit, gentle readers
stories.end: So what greater achievement could there be, Ajesha? Are you proud of me?
stories.caption: Savita Bhabhi’s favourite blog
stories.kicker: Amit Varma recalls his blogging days
stories.head: Bhabhi bookmarks India Uncut
body: Ajay Shah introduced it as “one of the highlights of Amit Varma’s life”. Around 2006 or 2007, an adult comic called *Savita Bhabhi* was becoming popular; its heroine had wild adventures with visiting plumbers and ladies’ tailors.
Varma was then running India Uncut, a hugely popular blog: some 8,000 posts in five years, about five a day. {#posts}
~ He wrote about the comic, and likes to think he was one of the reasons it exploded and went viral, in the days before Twitter. {#viral}
Then one day he opened the latest edition to find its heroine discussing her favourite blog. It was India Uncut. “So what greater achievement could there be, Ajay Shah?” he asked. {126-S03}
stories.why: Before Twitter, virality ran through blogs, and a popular blogger could lift an underground comic as surely as the comic could return the favour. Varma tells it with self-mocking pride.
stories.postscript: Varma also wrote a naughty version of *My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean* for the Bengali boudi: “My Boudi Lies Over the Lotion.” {126-J06}

stories.start: there is one interesting story I have to tell about this
stories.end: our bodies are hardwired in all of these different ways
stories.caption: ovulation and the lap dancers
stories.kicker: What the body knows before the mind does
stories.head: A monthly tipping point
body: Just before his talk at the Goa meetup, Amit Varma promised a group of women: “Ladies, I’m gonna go up there and I’m gonna mansplain to you about ovulation.” {126-J09}

The finding: ovulating women, whether they know it or not, tend to dress more revealingly and be more open to bad-boy types. Among lap dancers, the ovulating earned by far the highest tips and the menstruating the least. {#tips} Whether the dancers behaved differently or the men sensed something, nobody knows.

Most striking to Varma, men grew more protective of their partners during ovulation, though they have no way of knowing it. “There is something happening at a subliminal instinctive level which we are not even aware of,” he said. {126-S05}
~ In a blind smell test, women found the most dominant, high-status men the sexiest by body odour. {#smell}
stories.why: Much mating behaviour, Varma suggested, runs on signals that neither sender nor receiver consciously perceives. The body keeps its own calendar beneath awareness, which is one more reason, in his telling, to study our wiring rather than deny it.

stories.start: Because what happened here was we launched this course.
stories.end: where I just felt immediately at ease and comfortable with each and every person.
stories.caption: the Goa meetup
stories.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on their Life Lessons meetup
stories.head: Fifty came, seven on sabbatical
body: After three cohorts of their course Life Lessons in 2025, with some 130 participants, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah planned a meetup in Goa and hoped for 20 or 30 people. Between 50 and 60 came, booking their own flights and hotels. {#fiftysixty}
At the first lunch, the first seven people to join Varma were all on sabbatical. {#sabbatical} He credits a selection effect: a premium price and serious content drew curious people with agency.
Varma calls himself a socially awkward introvert whom large crowds make uncomfortable. Yet in Goa he felt at ease with everyone. {126-S01}

~ Last-minute sign-ups arrived, Shah said, one from Thailand and one from New York. {#thailand} Varma blamed the FOMO in the course’s WhatsApp group, and recalled singing, dancing and a man with a ukulele.

quote.text: this was the only gathering in my life where I just felt immediately at ease and comfortable with each and every person.

quiz.q: How many questions did Alfred Kinsey put to his respondents, by Amit Varma’s account?
quiz.a: Five hundred and twenty-one, to many thousands of people in elite Westernised society.

quiz.q: Which blog did the heroine of the comic *Savita Bhabhi* name as her favourite?
quiz.a: India Uncut, Amit Varma’s own blog, which ran some 8,000 posts in five years.

quiz.q: What do Ogas and Gaddam call the set of four detectives in women’s minds?
quiz.a: Miss Marple’s Detective Agency: social, cultural, emotional and physical detectives vetting potential mates.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, is it far harder to turn on a woman than a man?
quiz.a: Male arousal runs on the power of or; female arousal needs the power of and.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s shoe-size example teach about generalisations concerning men and women?
quiz.a: Something can be true on average without being anyone’s essential identity.

quiz.q: Whose line did Varma close with, about the desire of the man and of the woman?
quiz.a: Madame de Staël’s: the woman’s desire is for the desire of the man.
